messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Walter Mendez had spent much of his life trying to appear unremarkable, a careful habit learned in childhood and carried into his long career as an insurance agent. He grew up with a caregiver who could turn without warning from sternness to physical abuse, and what he remembered most was not only the pain but the betrayal of it: the person who was supposed to protect him was the one who hurt him. Now, at 71, he described those early years as the place where he learned that his body could not be trusted. Even on ordinary days, he felt that his body kept reacting as if danger were still present, and he was angry that the people responsible had faced no consequences. 

Certain moments in the present cut through his composure with unusual force. If a stranger approached him on the street or struck up conversation in a waiting room, Walter immediately felt threatened, as if the person’s friendliness might conceal harm. The same surge came when he heard sirens passing outside his apartment or caught the smell of alcohol on someone in a store or elevator. Those moments did not just startle him; they seemed to confirm what he had come to believe about himself and the world, that he was still vulnerable and that others could not be trusted. The triggers fed his sense that the old injustice had never been corrected, and that left him watching strangers more closely and bracing whenever a siren wailed down the block. 

Walter also found that his memories did not stay in the past where he wanted them. Fragments of the childhood abuse would appear without warning and disappear just as quickly, sometimes brought on by a smell he could not avoid, and when he thought about the frightening event he could sometimes smell the same things he had smelled back then. Those memories felt more real and vivid to him than memories of ordinary things; they arrived with a physical force that made the events seem immediate rather than distant. When they came, they reinforced his belief that his body was still acting as if he were in danger and that he had been betrayed by someone he trusted. They also sharpened his reaction to the present: a stranger walking too close, the faint odor of alcohol on a passerby, or a siren outside his building could suddenly feel charged with the old threat. 

To manage this, Walter had built a life around staying mentally busy. He kept his mind occupied all the time, filling gaps in the day with work tasks, lists, and constant internal chatter. He also performed private mental rituals, telling himself certain phrases in hopes of preventing bad things from happening again, and he avoided television programs, films, or reading about similar events because anything resembling the abuse could pull up the images and sensations he feared most. In the short term these habits gave him a sense of control, but they also kept him on edge. The more he tried to monitor every possibility of harm and hold disaster at bay, the more convinced he became that danger was close. His mind never settled, and his vigilance made strangers, sirens, and alcohol smell feel even more like warnings than coincidences. 

Over time, the cycle narrowed his world. At his office, where he had once spoken easily with clients, he began avoiding unnecessary conversation with unfamiliar people, letting colleagues handle walk-ins when he could. He listened for sounds that might mean someone was entering his home, especially at night, and sat tense in the evenings, scanning for anything unusual. When a siren passed, he would freeze briefly, and when he caught the smell of alcohol near the grocery store or in the lobby of his building, he would leave quickly, feeling as though his own body had already decided there was something to fear. Each of these moments seemed to confirm his appraisals: that he had been betrayed, that no one had paid for what happened, and that his body’s alarm system was not merely overactive but still necessary. 

Walter finally sought help after noticing how much of his day was now organized around not being caught off guard. He was tired of living in a state of constant readiness, tired of the rituals and the scanning, and worried that his world was shrinking further. What he most feared was that he would never feel safe even in his own apartment, yet what he hoped for was simpler: to be able to hear a siren, pass a stranger, or catch the smell of alcohol without feeling as if the past had become present again.
